t.2.70.1: To Bharata, son of Kekayī, thus burning with grief, the sage Vasiṣṭha, best of speakers and excellent in speech, spoke.
t.2.70.2: Enough of grief, bless you, O prince of great renown! The time has come; carry out the final journey of the lord of men.
t.2.70.3: Having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, Bharata, knower of dharma, regained his composure and had all the funeral rites for the departed performed.
t.2.70.5: Having laid Daśaratha upon an excellent bed adorned with many kinds of jewels, his son, deeply grieved, then lamented.
t.2.70.4: He then looked upon the king, who had been lifted out of the soaking oil and laid upon the ground, his face gone a pale yellow hue, lying there as though asleep.
t.2.70.6: O king, what was it that you resolved upon while I was away and had not yet returned, banishing Rāma, the knower of dharma, and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa?
t.2.70.7: Where will you go, great king, abandoning these grieving people, who are bereft of Rāma, that lion among men, whose deeds are never wearisome to him?
t.2.70.8: But who, O king, will secure your welfare in this city, now that you, father, have departed to heaven and Rāma has taken refuge in the forest?
t.2.70.9: O king, bereft of you, the widowed earth no longer shines; the city appears to me like a night without its moon.
t.2.70.10: To Bharata, who was lamenting thus with a dejected heart, the great sage Vasiṣṭha spoke words once more.
t.2.70.11: O mighty-armed one, whatever funeral rites must be performed for this lord of the people, let them be carried out calmly and without hesitation.
t.2.70.12: Saying "So be it," Bharata honored those words of Vasiṣṭha and urged on the officiating priests, the family priests and the teachers in every way.
t.2.70.14: Then the attendants, their throats choked with tears and their minds distraught, placed the unconscious king upon a palanquin and carried him away.
t.2.70.13: And the sacred fires that had been brought out of the fire-sanctuary are carried before the king by the officiating priests and sacrificers, according to the prescribed rite.
t.2.70.15: Strewing the road with gold, both coined and uncoined, and with garments of many kinds, the people went on ahead of the king.
t.2.70.16: Others, likewise, brought sandalwood, the resins of aguru, sarala, padmaka, and devadāru woods, and built the funeral pyre.
t.2.70.17: Having placed there various fragrances of every kind, both high and low, the officiating priests then laid that lord of the earth down in the midst of the funeral pyre.
t.2.70.18: Then, having made offerings into the fire, his priests murmured their prayers, and the singers of the Sāman chanted the Sāman hymns there in accordance with the scriptures.
t.2.70.19: Then his wives went out from the city there in palanquins and carriages, as befitted their rank, surrounded by the elders.
t.2.70.21: There was heard the cry of women by the thousands, stricken with grief, wailing piteously at that time like female krauñca birds.
t.2.70.20: Then the priests, and the women led by Kausalyā, burning with grief, circled leftward around the king who had been laid upon the fire.
t.2.70.22: Then the noble ladies, weeping and helpless, lamenting again and again, descended from their carriages onto the bank of the Sarayū.
t.2.70.23: After the water offering had been made, they, the king's wives, the ministers and the priests, together with Bharata, entered the city with eyes filled with tears, and for ten days they passed their time in sorrow, lying upon the ground.
